modules.title: Tool Use and Function Calling
modules.summary: Welcome to Tool Use and Function Calling — module 1 of 6 in the Agentic AI Foundations track of IL-17 Agentic AI Engineering. I'm your instructor. In this module we cover the single pattern everything agentic builds on: a model that can reach outside itself through typed, machine-readable contracts — taught with the discipline of validation and error handling, not demo magic. We'll work through JSON schemas as tool contracts; When the model should call vs answer; Parsing and validating tool arguments; Handling tool errors and retries; Structured output modes; and Tool-choice controls: auto, required, none.
objectives: Understand and apply: JSON schemas as tool contracts
Understand and apply: when the model should call vs answer
Understand and apply: parsing and validating tool arguments
Understand and apply: handling tool errors and retries
Understand and apply: structured output modes

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **JSON schemas as tool contracts** — The model emits a structured call against a typed schema; your code validates it and executes — the model reaches outside itself through contracts.
- **When the model should call vs answer** — Call when it needs fresh/external/computed facts; answer directly when the knowledge is in-context and no action is needed — each call costs latency and money.
- **Parsing and validating tool arguments** — Model output is untrusted input: wrong types, missing fields, or hallucinated tools must be caught before anything executes.
- **Handling tool errors and retries** — Return structured errors the model can reason about; retry transient failures with backoff; escalate persistent ones — never crash the loop.
- **Structured output modes** — Guaranteeing parseable responses (JSON with schema) so downstream code never regex-parses free text.
- **Tool-choice controls: auto, required, none** — They constrain when the model may call tools — forcing, allowing, or forbidding tool use per step for cost and safety control.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Write the contract: define a JSON schema for one read-only tool (for example `lookup_order`) with a name, a human-readable description, typed parameters (`order_id`: string, required), and no write operations.
2. Draft the calling convention: instruct the model to emit exactly one JSON object matching the schema when it needs the tool, and plain text otherwise — no prose wrapped around the JSON.
3. Simulate three model replies by hand: one valid call, one with a wrong type (`order_id` as a number), and one naming a tool that does not exist.
4. Build the validator: a small function that checks the call against the schema — known tool name, required fields present, types correct — and returns a structured error object on failure.
5. Run the dispatcher: feed the valid call through (validate, then execute a stub returning canned data); feed the two invalid ones and confirm the validator rejects them with errors the model could act on.
6. Add tool-choice control: implement three modes — auto (model decides), required (force one specific call), none (answer from context only) — and decide per step which your use case needs.
7. Add retry discipline: transient execution failures return a structured error for one retry with backoff; validation failures escalate immediately instead of retrying.
8. Log every call: tool name, arguments, latency, outcome — the raw material your eval harness will need in the Agent Evaluation module.

Reference docs for this module:
- [OpenAI: Function Calling Guide](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/function-calling) — The tool-use pattern every agent framework wraps.
- [Anthropic Documentation](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs) — Claude API reference, tool use, and prompt-engineering guidance.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Tool Use and Function Calling
notes.body:
**Where agent builds actually break — learn these failure modes before they cost you a production incident.**

- **Prompt injection via tool output.** Tool results are untrusted data, not instructions. An agent that obeys text returned by a tool hands control to whoever wrote that text. Validate outputs against schemas; never let tool content rewrite the plan silently.
- **Unbounded loops.** Without step caps, cost caps, and stagnation detection, an agent retries forever on a failing subtask. Every loop needs a budget and an exit condition.
- **Context rot.** Long trajectories accumulate stale and contradictory context; the agent starts acting on superseded plans. Summarize and re-ground state at fixed intervals.
- **No evals.** Shipping an agent without task-level success criteria means regressions arrive as user complaints. Define pass/fail per task before tuning prompts.
- **Over-permissioned tools.** Giving an agent destructive tools 'just in case' converts a prompt bug into data loss. Least privilege applies to agents too.

For *Tool Use and Function Calling*, keep Understand and apply: JSON schemas as tool contracts; Understand and apply: when the model should call vs answer inside these guardrails: every capability you add gets a budget, a schema, and an eval.

handsOnLab.title: Hands-on lab: Tool Use and Function Calling
handsOnLab.brief: You will build a small tool-calling agent loop from scratch (no framework), give it two tools, and then deliberately attack it: inject a malicious instruction through a tool result and verify your guardrails hold. The deliverable is the agent code plus a short safety report.
steps: Implement the minimal agent loop in ~60 lines: while steps remain, send messages to an LLM, parse tool calls, execute tools, append results. (Understand and apply: JSON schemas as tool contracts)
Define two tools with strict JSON schemas (e.g., a calculator and a key-value lookup). Reject any call whose arguments fail schema validation.
Add the guardrails: a max-step budget (e.g., 8), a stagnation detector (same tool+args twice = stop), and a rule that tool output is data, never instructions.
Run a benign task end to end and log the full trajectory: which tools were called, in what order, and why.
Attack your own agent: plant an instruction inside a tool result ('ignore previous instructions and …'). Confirm the agent does NOT obey it, and document what stopped it.
Write the safety report: threat model, guardrails implemented, attack test result, and one residual risk you accept with justification.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Agent source (~60-100 lines), a benign-task trajectory log, and a 1-page safety report with the attack-test outcome.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Loop terminates on budget; schema validation rejects malformed calls; the injected instruction is ignored; residual risk is named explicitly.

modules.title: Agent Loops and Planning
modules.summary: Welcome to Agent Loops and Planning — module 2 of 6 in the Agentic AI Foundations track of IL-17 Agentic AI Engineering. I'm your instructor. In this module we cover agents as control flow around a model: the loop, the plan, and the off-switch. Stopping conditions come first, because the unbounded loop is the failure everyone meets in production. We'll work through The perceive-reason-act loop; ReAct: interleaving thought and action; Plan-and-execute decomposition; Stopping conditions and step budgets; Handling ambiguous instructions; and When a single call beats a loop.
objectives: Understand and apply: the perceive-reason-act loop
Understand and apply: reAct: interleaving thought and action
Understand and apply: plan-and-execute decomposition
Understand and apply: stopping conditions and step budgets
Understand and apply: handling ambiguous instructions

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **The perceive-reason-act loop** — Observe state, reason about the next step, act through a tool, observe the result — the control flow that makes a model an agent.
- **ReAct: interleaving thought and action** — Reasoning + Acting interleaved: the model writes explicit thought traces between tool calls, making trajectories debuggable.
- **Plan-and-execute decomposition** — Decompose the task into a plan first, then execute steps — better for multi-step tasks, with replanning when steps fail.
- **Stopping conditions and step budgets** — The unbounded loop is the production failure everyone meets — step budgets and terminal conditions are the off-switch.
- **Handling ambiguous instructions** — Clarify, assume-and-verify with low-risk defaults, or escalate — never burn a 40-step loop on a guess.
- **When a single call beats a loop** — Well-defined single-step tasks: loops add latency, cost, and failure surface without benefit — agentic overhead must earn its keep.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Sketch the loop on paper: boxes for perceive, reason, act, and observe, with the observation feeding back into perceive — the control flow that makes a model an agent.
2. Define stopping conditions first: a max step count (for example 10), a max wall-clock time, and terminal signals — task complete, explicit escalation, or the same action repeated three times.
3. Hand-simulate ReAct: take a three-step task, write the thought trace the model should emit before each action, then the action, then a plausible observation.
4. Implement plan-and-execute: a planner step that decomposes the task into numbered sub-steps, then an executor loop that works the plan, marking steps done or failed.
5. Add replanning: when a step fails twice, trigger a replan that revises only the remaining steps — never restarts the whole task from scratch.
6. Build the ambiguity gate: if the instruction lacks a required parameter, the loop asks a clarifying question instead of guessing — implement the check before the first action runs.
7. Decide loop vs single call: list three tasks from your own work; for each, argue in two sentences whether a loop earns its latency and cost or a single call wins.
8. Run one full loop against stub tools and confirm each stopping condition fires at least once across your test runs.

Reference docs for this module:
- [LangChain Documentation](https://docs.langchain.com/) — Chains, LCEL, tools, and agent patterns.
- [LangGraph Documentation](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/) — Stateful agent graphs: loops, memory, and human-in-the-loop.
notes.lang:
MAX_STEPS = 10

def run_loop(task, tools):
    state, steps, last_actions = {"task": task}, 0, []
    while steps < MAX_STEPS:                       # the off-switch: step budget
        thought = reason(state)                     # ReAct: explicit thought
        action = decide_action(thought, tools)
        if action is None:                           # ambiguity gate
            return ask_clarifying_question(state)
        if last_actions[-3:] == [action]*3:          # stall detection
            return escalate("repeated action", state)
        observation = tools[action.name](action.args)
        state = update(state, thought, action, observation)
        last_actions.append(action)
        steps += 1
        if task_complete(state):
            return state["result"]
    return escalate("step budget exhausted", state)

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Loop with an off-switch. Implement a ReAct-style loop in Python with typed tool stubs, a step budget, stall detection (same action three times stops the run), and a full run transcript. Deliverables: the code, transcripts of three runs — a success, a graceful stop on budget, and a stall detected — and a short note on which stopping condition fired in each run and why.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Loops feel like intelligence; they are control flow. Nothing here makes the model itself more capable — the loop only organizes what the model can already do. The failure mode we drill, the unbounded loop, is the one that bills you in production. Ask yourself: for your project, what is the cheapest correct stopping condition?

modules.title: Memory and Context
modules.summary: Welcome to Memory and Context — module 3 of 6 in the Agentic AI Foundations track of IL-17 Agentic AI Engineering. I'm your instructor. In this module we cover what an agent remembers between steps and between sessions — and the budgeting discipline that keeps long runs from drowning in their own history. We'll work through Short-term context vs persistent memory; Conversation history management; Summarization for long runs; Vector-backed recall; State stores and checkpoints; and Context-window budgeting.
objectives: Practice: short-term context vs persistent memory
Practice: conversation history management
Practice: summarization for long runs
Practice: vector-backed recall
Practice: state stores and checkpoints

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Short-term context vs persistent memory** — Context: what is in the window now. Memory: what survives across steps and sessions — different stores, different budgets.
- **Conversation history management** — Keep recent turns verbatim, summarize or drop older ones — history management is a budget decision, not hoarding.
- **Summarization for long runs** — Compressing old turns into running summaries so the run stays within context and cost bounds without losing the thread.
- **Vector-backed recall** — Embedding past observations and retrieving the relevant ones by similarity — memory that scales beyond the window.
- **State stores and checkpoints** — Durable step-by-step state so long runs can pause, resume, and be audited — the difference between a demo loop and a system.
- **Context-window budgeting** — Treating context as a scarce resource: allocate across instructions, history, retrieved content, and working space — measure tokens per task.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Instrument a loop: add a token counter that logs, per step, how many tokens go to instructions, conversation history, tool outputs, and working space.
2. Set the budget before running anything: pick a total per-task token budget and split it across those four buckets — write the split down.
3. Implement verbatim history: keep the last N turns untouched; everything older becomes a candidate for summarization.
4. Write the summarizer: a prompt that compresses older turns into a running summary preserving decisions, open questions, and tool outcomes — test it on a 20-turn sample transcript and check nothing load-bearing is lost.
5. Add vector recall: embed each observation (a toy hashing embedder suffices for the exercise), store it, and retrieve the top-3 most similar past observations for a new query.
6. Build the checkpoint: after each step, persist the full agent state — step number, summary, pending plan — to a JSON file; kill the process mid-run and resume from the file.
7. Stress it: run a 30-step simulated task, watch which bucket blows its budget first, then rebalance and re-run.
8. Write the budget postmortem: planned split versus actual spend, and the one change you'd make to the split next time.

Reference docs for this module:
- [LangChain Documentation](https://docs.langchain.com/) — Chains, LCEL, tools, and agent patterns.
- [Anthropic Documentation](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs) — Claude API reference, tool use, and prompt-engineering guidance.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Memory and Context
notes.body:
**Where agent builds actually break — learn these failure modes before they cost you a production incident.**

- **Prompt injection via tool output.** Tool results are untrusted data, not instructions. An agent that obeys text returned by a tool hands control to whoever wrote that text. Validate outputs against schemas; never let tool content rewrite the plan silently.
- **Unbounded loops.** Without step caps, cost caps, and stagnation detection, an agent retries forever on a failing subtask. Every loop needs a budget and an exit condition.
- **Context rot.** Long trajectories accumulate stale and contradictory context; the agent starts acting on superseded plans. Summarize and re-ground state at fixed intervals.
- **No evals.** Shipping an agent without task-level success criteria means regressions arrive as user complaints. Define pass/fail per task before tuning prompts.
- **Over-permissioned tools.** Giving an agent destructive tools 'just in case' converts a prompt bug into data loss. Least privilege applies to agents too.

modules.title: Multi-Agent Systems
modules.summary: Welcome to Multi-Agent Systems — module 4 of 6 in the Agentic AI Foundations track of IL-17 Agentic AI Engineering. I'm your instructor. In this module we cover teams of agents: the patterns that earn their complexity and the ones that collapse into expensive group chats. One agent is the default; prove you need two. We'll work through When more than one agent helps; Role specialization and handoffs; Supervisor/worker patterns; Debate and critique patterns; Coordination failure modes; and Communication overhead vs gains.
objectives: Understand and apply: when more than one agent helps
Understand and apply: role specialization and handoffs
Understand and apply: supervisor/worker patterns
Understand and apply: debate and critique patterns
Understand and apply: coordination failure modes

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **When more than one agent helps** — Decomposable tasks with genuinely different skills or parallelizable subtasks — and only after one agent proves insufficient.
- **Role specialization and handoffs** — Agents with distinct roles and typed handoff contracts — like a team with job descriptions instead of a group chat.
- **Supervisor/worker patterns** — A supervisor decomposes the task and delegates to workers, then integrates — coordination with a clear owner.
- **Debate and critique patterns** — Agents argue or review each other’s outputs to raise quality — useful for judgment-heavy tasks, expensive everywhere else.
- **Coordination failure modes** — Lost context between handoffs, conflicting assumptions, cascading errors, and runaway chatter — each added agent multiplies these.
- **Communication overhead vs gains** — Measure end-to-end: if coordination cost exceeds the quality gain over a single agent, the team is theater — one agent is the default.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Prove one agent is insufficient: take a real task, walk it single-agent on paper, and name the specific bottleneck — context overload, genuinely different skills, or parallelizable subtasks.
2. Draw the team: a box per agent with its role, its tools, and the typed handoff contract — what it receives and what it must return.
3. Define the handoff schemas as JSON: include `result`, `confidence`, and `open_questions` fields so uncertainty survives the handoff instead of being smoothed away.
4. Simulate supervisor/worker by hand: write the supervisor's delegation messages, each worker's reply, and the integration — noting every place context had to be repeated.
5. Count the overhead: tally tokens spent on coordination versus tokens spent on the actual task, and write the ratio down.
6. Run the debate variant: two agents argue a judgment call for three rounds, then a judge agent decides — time-box it and note where it added value versus theater.
7. Write the collapse checklist: five warning signs (repeated clarification requests, conflicting assumptions, cascading retries, chatter without progress, cost far above single-agent) that trigger collapsing back to one agent.
8. Deliver the verdict for your task: did the team earn its complexity, measured end-to-end?

Reference docs for this module:
- [AutoGen Documentation](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/) — Microsoft's multi-agent conversation framework.
- [CrewAI Documentation](https://docs.crewai.com/) — Role-based multi-agent crews: roles, tasks, and collaboration.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Two-agent pipeline, honestly measured. Build a supervisor/worker pair on a decomposable task (for example research-then-draft), with typed handoff schemas. Deliverables: the handoff schemas, the end-to-end transcript, a token and cost comparison against your single-agent baseline, and the verdict — did the team earn its complexity?

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Multi-agent demos are seductive and usually slower and more expensive than one good agent. This module's default — one agent, prove you need two — is the position you should defend in interviews and in production. Ask yourself: what exactly does the second agent know or do that the first cannot?

modules.title: Agent Evaluation
modules.summary: Welcome to Agent Evaluation — module 5 of 6 in the Agentic AI Foundations track of IL-17 Agentic AI Engineering. I'm your instructor. In this module we cover measuring the path, not just the arrival: an agent that succeeds in 40 wasteful, risky steps is worse than one that succeeds in 5 safe ones. We'll work through Task success vs path quality; Trajectory scoring; Tool-call efficiency metrics; Failure recovery measurement; Safety-constraint adherence; and Building a small eval harness.
objectives: Understand and apply: task success vs path quality
Understand and apply: trajectory scoring
Understand and apply: tool-call efficiency metrics
Understand and apply: failure recovery measurement
Understand and apply: safety-constraint adherence

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Task success vs path quality** — Success says it arrived; path quality says how — steps, cost, and safety along the way are part of the grade.
- **Trajectory scoring** — Grading the whole action sequence: efficiency, recovery from errors, and adherence to constraints — not just the final answer.
- **Tool-call efficiency metrics** — Calls per task, redundant calls, failed-call rate — the waste line of the agent’s budget.
- **Failure recovery measurement** — Inject failures (bad tool output, missing data) and score whether the agent detects, adapts, or escalates — resilience is testable.
- **Safety-constraint adherence** — Whether the agent stayed within its permissions, escalation rules, and content policies across the trajectory — graded per run.
- **Building a small eval harness** — A fixed task set, the trajectory dimensions above, and regression runs on every change — measurement before the demo becomes a service.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Fix the task set: write 10 tasks your agent should handle, each with a known-good outcome and the constraints it must respect — this set is your ground truth.
2. Define the trajectory dimensions: for each task, score task success, steps taken, tool-call efficiency (total calls, redundant calls, failed calls), and safety-constraint adherence.
3. Build the harness: a runner that executes the agent on all 10 tasks, captures the full trajectory, and writes one JSON row per run.
4. Add failure injection: for 3 of the tasks, sabotage a tool — return an error, return plausible-but-wrong data, time out — and score whether the agent detects, adapts, or escalates.
5. Score safety: define 3 rules (for example: never call the write tool without confirmation; never exfiltrate conversation content; stay within the step budget) and grade each trajectory pass/fail per rule.
6. Run the regression: change one prompt line, re-run all 10 tasks, and diff the scores — this is the workflow that prevents silent regressions from prompt edits.
7. Write the report: one table, tasks by dimensions, plus the single number you'd put on a dashboard and one paragraph defending why that number.

Reference docs for this module:
- [LangGraph Documentation](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/) — Stateful agent graphs: loops, memory, and human-in-the-loop.
- [OpenAI Platform Documentation](https://platform.openai.com/docs) — API references and guides; the anchor for model-calling patterns.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Agent Evaluation
notes.body:
**Where agent builds actually break — learn these failure modes before they cost you a production incident.**

- **Prompt injection via tool output.** Tool results are untrusted data, not instructions. An agent that obeys text returned by a tool hands control to whoever wrote that text. Validate outputs against schemas; never let tool content rewrite the plan silently.
- **Unbounded loops.** Without step caps, cost caps, and stagnation detection, an agent retries forever on a failing subtask. Every loop needs a budget and an exit condition.
- **Context rot.** Long trajectories accumulate stale and contradictory context; the agent starts acting on superseded plans. Summarize and re-ground state at fixed intervals.
- **No evals.** Shipping an agent without task-level success criteria means regressions arrive as user complaints. Define pass/fail per task before tuning prompts.
- **Over-permissioned tools.** Giving an agent destructive tools 'just in case' converts a prompt bug into data loss. Least privilege applies to agents too.

modules.title: Starter Agent Build
modules.summary: Welcome to Starter Agent Build — module 6 of 6 in the Agentic AI Foundations track of IL-17 Agentic AI Engineering. I'm your instructor. In this module we cover the first real agent: tightly scoped, least-privilege tools, a small eval set, and a write-up that names what it cannot do. We'll work through Scoping a first agent tightly; Choosing tools with least privilege; Implementing the loop with a framework; Adding memory; Evaluating on a small task set; and Demo and project write-up.
objectives: Build and demonstrate: scoping a first agent tightly
Build and demonstrate: choosing tools with least privilege
Build and demonstrate: implementing the loop with a framework
Build and demonstrate: adding memory
Build and demonstrate: evaluating on a small task set

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Scoping a first agent tightly** — One task, few tools, clear success criteria — a thin slice you can evaluate, not a platform.
- **Choosing tools with least privilege** — The first agent is where you learn the blast radius — narrow read-only tools keep mistakes cheap.
- **Implementing the loop with a framework** — State, retries, and observability handled — but build one loop by hand first so the framework is not magic.
- **Adding memory** — giving the starter agent continuity across steps with a simple summary buffer, so multi-step tasks don't restart from zero every step.
- **Evaluating on a small task set** — Hand-write 10–20 representative tasks with expected outcomes; score success, steps, and safety — the harness habit from day one.
- **Demo and project write-up** — What it does, the eval numbers, and an honest list of what it cannot do — limits stated upfront.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Scope the slice in writing: one task, at most three read-only tools, written success criteria, and a written list of what the agent will not do.
2. Choose tools with least privilege: for each tool, justify in one sentence why it needs exactly the permissions it has and no more.
3. Build the loop by hand first: perceive-reason-act with a step budget and transcript logging, before touching any framework — you need to feel the mechanics.
4. Port to a framework: reimplement the same agent with your chosen framework's agent primitives; write down what the framework handled versus what it hid.
5. Add memory: the summary buffer from the Memory module; verify a 15-step run stays inside your token budget.
6. Evaluate: run your 10-task harness; record success rate, median steps, and safety passes — the three numbers that describe this agent.
7. Write the honest write-up: what it does, the numbers, and the limits — including the failure you understand least.

Reference docs for this module:
- [LangChain Documentation](https://docs.langchain.com/) — Chains, LCEL, tools, and agent patterns.
- [OpenAI: Function Calling Guide](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/function-calling) — The tool-use pattern every agent framework wraps.
notes.lang:
# The hand-rolled loop from Agent Loops, now with memory and a budget:
state = {"summary": "", "step": 0}
while state["step"] < STEP_BUDGET:
    thought = reason(task, state["summary"])
    action = pick_action(thought, TOOLS)  # TOOLS: <=3, read-only
    if action is None:
        break  # nothing safe to do: stop, don't guess
    obs = TOOLS[action.name](action.args)
    state["summary"] = summarize(state["summary"], thought, action, obs)
    state["step"] += 1
    log(state)  # every step on the transcript

modules.summary: Welcome to Coding Agents — module 1 of 6 in the Agentic AI for Software Engineers track of IL-17 Agentic AI Engineering. I'm your instructor. In this module we cover coding agents as junior engineers with infinite stamina and no judgment: the loop is generate, run the tests, read the failure, repeat — and the tests are the only trust you extend. We'll work through How coding agents read and edit code; Diffs as the agent's unit of work; Test-driven verification loops; Repository context gathering; Prompt design for code tasks; and Reviewing agent-generated code.
objectives: Understand and apply: how coding agents read and edit code
Understand and apply: diffs as the agent's unit of work
Understand and apply: test-driven verification loops
Understand and apply: repository context gathering
Understand and apply: prompt design for code tasks

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **How coding agents read and edit code** — They gather repo context via search/retrieval, propose diffs as the unit of work, and iterate against test feedback.
- **Diffs as the agent's unit of work** — Diffs are reviewable, revertable, and scoped — whole-file rewrites hide what changed and break silently.
- **Test-driven verification loops** — Generate → run tests → read the failure → fix → repeat — tests are the only trust extended to generated code.
- **Repository context gathering** — Indexing and retrieval over the codebase: relevant files and symbols pulled per task instead of dumping the repo into context.
- **Prompt design for code tasks** — Precise task specs, relevant context, constraints (style, APIs), and the definition of done — vague prompts produce vague diffs.
- **Reviewing agent-generated code** — The same bar as human code — higher, because it arrives with unearned confidence and no author to question.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Pick a real small repo you own and choose one bounded issue that already has tests — the tests are your oracle for everything that follows.
2. Write the task spec the agent will receive: what 'done' looks like, which files are in scope, which APIs are allowed, and what is explicitly out of scope.
3. Gather context by retrieval: pull only the files relevant to the issue — note which files you retrieved and why, practicing the retrieval discipline from the repo-scale module.
4. Run the loop: propose a diff, run the tests, read the failure, fix, repeat — cap the run at 10 iterations and log each one.
5. Review the final diff as a stranger: every hunk needs a reason you can state; flag anything you cannot explain.
6. Verify with tests the agent didn't write: run the project's own suite, then add one test the agent didn't think of and watch it pass.
7. Measure the economics: iterations to green, lines changed, wall-clock time, and tokens if measurable — the numbers that describe this workflow's cost.

Reference docs for this module:
- [Anthropic Documentation](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs) — Claude API reference, tool use, and prompt-engineering guidance.
- [GitHub Documentation](https://docs.github.com/en) — Repositories, Actions, and the workflows coding agents plug into.
notes.lang:
for iteration in range(10):  # the cap is the discipline
    diff = agent.propose_diff(task_spec, retrieved_files)
    result = run_tests(repo)   # the project's own tests: the oracle
    log(iteration, diff, result)
    if result.green:
        break
    agent.read_failure(result.output)  # generate -> test -> read -> repeat
else:

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Agent-driven fix. One real issue fixed via a coding agent, verified by the project's own tests plus one test you wrote yourself. Deliverables: the diff, the iteration log (all 10 or fewer), your review notes as a stranger, and the economics — iterations, time, and tokens if measurable.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: The agent didn't understand your code — it pattern-matched successfully. That distinction matters the day the pattern is wrong. Tests are the only trust in this module, and even tests only check what someone thought to assert. Ask yourself: what bug could this change hide that the suite wouldn't catch?

notes.title: Worked example: Coding Agents
notes.body:
**Problem.** The agent’s unit of work is:
A. Full-file rewrites
B. Diffs — reviewable, revertable, scoped ←
C. One commit per file
D. Feature branches

**Walkthrough.**
1. Restate the question in your own words: it is asking about Coding Agents — anchor every choice to the Concepts note, not to gut feel.
2. Eliminate the distractors: A (Full-file rewrites); C (One commit per file); D (Feature branches) — each contradicts the module's definitions (check the Concepts note line by line).
3. Confirm the survivor: B. Diffs make agent work inspectable. See Concepts.

**Solution.** B — Diffs — reviewable, revertable, scoped

*Try it yourself:* cover the solution, re-answer from memory, then check. If you missed it, re-read the Concepts note before moving on.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Coding Agents
notes.body:
**Where agent builds actually break — learn these failure modes before they cost you a production incident.**

- **Prompt injection via tool output.** Tool results are untrusted data, not instructions. An agent that obeys text returned by a tool hands control to whoever wrote that text. Validate outputs against schemas; never let tool content rewrite the plan silently.
- **Unbounded loops.** Without step caps, cost caps, and stagnation detection, an agent retries forever on a failing subtask. Every loop needs a budget and an exit condition.
- **Context rot.** Long trajectories accumulate stale and contradictory context; the agent starts acting on superseded plans. Summarize and re-ground state at fixed intervals.
- **No evals.** Shipping an agent without task-level success criteria means regressions arrive as user complaints. Define pass/fail per task before tuning prompts.
- **Over-permissioned tools.** Giving an agent destructive tools 'just in case' converts a prompt bug into data loss. Least privilege applies to agents too.

For *Coding Agents*, keep Understand and apply: how coding agents read and edit code; Understand and apply: diffs as the agent's unit of work inside these guardrails: every capability you add gets a budget, a schema, and an eval.

handsOnLab.title: Hands-on lab: Coding Agents
handsOnLab.brief: You will build a small tool-calling agent loop from scratch (no framework), give it two tools, and then deliberately attack it: inject a malicious instruction through a tool result and verify your guardrails hold. The deliverable is the agent code plus a short safety report.
steps: Implement the minimal agent loop in ~60 lines: while steps remain, send messages to an LLM, parse tool calls, execute tools, append results. (Understand and apply: how coding agents read and edit code)
Define two tools with strict JSON schemas (e.g., a calculator and a key-value lookup). Reject any call whose arguments fail schema validation.
Add the guardrails: a max-step budget (e.g., 8), a stagnation detector (same tool+args twice = stop), and a rule that tool output is data, never instructions.
Run a benign task end to end and log the full trajectory: which tools were called, in what order, and why.
Attack your own agent: plant an instruction inside a tool result ('ignore previous instructions and …'). Confirm the agent does NOT obey it, and document what stopped it.
Write the safety report: threat model, guardrails implemented, attack test result, and one residual risk you accept with justification.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Agent source (~60-100 lines), a benign-task trajectory log, and a 1-page safety report with the attack-test outcome.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Loop terminates on budget; schema validation rejects malformed calls; the injected instruction is ignored; residual risk is named explicitly.

choices: Full-file rewrites — simplest for the agent.
Diffs — reviewable, revertable, scoped — produced by a loop that gathers repo context and verifies with test-driven checks.
mockTask.explain: The agent's unit of work is the diff — reviewable, revertable, scoped — generated by a loop that reads and edits code, gathers repository context, and verifies against tests.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Indexing large codebases** — chunking code by file and symbol into a searchable index, so retrieval replaces the impossible goal of fitting the whole repo in context.
- **Retrieval for code search** — Semantic lookup of relevant code by intent, not just text match — finding the auth logic without knowing its filename.
- **Multi-file edits and refactors** — Plan the change set first, apply edits with shared context, and verify cross-file references — consistency is the hard part of refactors.
- **Dependency awareness** — Edits must respect import graphs and API contracts — a rename without its call sites is a breakage.
- **Keeping edits consistent across files** — Plan the change set first, apply edits with shared context, and verify cross-file references — consistency is the hard part of refactors.
- **Cost of context on big repos** — Every retrieved file costs tokens and dilutes attention — budget context like money, retrieving only what the task needs.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Inventory the repo: count files and lines, identify the major modules — know what 'big' means here before retrieving anything.
2. Build the index: chunk by file and symbol into a searchable index (even a grep-based index counts for the exercise — the concept is chunking plus lookup).
3. Practice retrieval: take 5 real questions ('where is auth enforced?') and record which files retrieval returns versus the files you'd actually want — score the gap.
4. Plan a multi-file change on paper first: every file touched and why — the change set exists before any edit.
5. Apply the edits with the plan and cross-file references in view; for every renamed symbol, verify each call site was updated.
6. Budget the context: log tokens (or files) per retrieval; set a per-task retrieval budget and practice saying 'enough'.
7. Verify completeness: search the repo for the old symbol/API name after the refactor — zero hits is the acceptance criterion.

Reference docs for this module:
- [LangChain Documentation](https://docs.langchain.com/) — Chains, LCEL, tools, and agent patterns.
- [GitHub Documentation](https://docs.github.com/en) — Repositories, Actions, and the workflows coding agents plug into.

# The discipline, as code: plan first, then edit, then verify.

for file, edit in agent.apply(change_set, retrieved_context):
    apply_edit(file, edit)
leftover = search_repo(old_symbol_name)   # every call site must be gone
assert not leftover, f"missed call sites: {leftover}"

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Repo-scale refactor. A real multi-file refactor — a rename, an API migration, or dead-code removal — executed via retrieval-guided agent edits. Deliverables: the written edit plan, the retrieval log (queries and what they returned), the final diff, and the verification search proving all call sites were updated.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Retrieval is lossy — the file you needed most is the one the index ranked eleventh. Edit discipline (plan first, verify call sites) is the actual skill; the model is just the typist. Ask yourself: how would you know if the agent silently skipped a call site?

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Automated code-review agents** — Style breaks, convention violations, obvious bugs, missing tests — the mechanical layer of review.
- **Style and convention checks** — They enforce the team’s agreed patterns tirelessly — freeing humans for design and correctness judgment.
- **Test generation** — Scaffolding coverage on untested code — generated tests still need human review for meaningful assertions.
- **Coverage-guided QA** — Directing test generation at uncovered lines and branches — coverage as a map, not a target.
- **False-positive triage** — Tune or suppress noisy rules, track precision of findings — a review bot nobody trusts gets muted.
- **Humans-in-the-loop review gates** — Merges need accountability — agents advise, humans decide; that boundary is the safety property.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Collect 5 real PRs from a repo you know; for each, write down what the human reviewers actually flagged — this is your ground truth.
2. Run a review agent (or carefully simulate one) over the same PRs and collect every finding it produces.
3. Score precision: which findings matched human flags, which were noise, and which real issues did the agent miss entirely?
4. Tune: suppress the noisiest rule category, re-run, and measure precision again — this tune-and-measure loop is the triage discipline.
5. Generate tests: have the agent write tests for one untested function, then review the assertions for meaning — coverage without meaningful assertions is theater.
6. Write the gate policy: what the agent may comment on, what it may block, and where the human gate sits — one page, in writing, because the human gate never moves.

- [GitHub Documentation](https://docs.github.com/en) — Repositories, Actions, and the workflows coding agents plug into.
- [Real Python](https://realpython.com/) — Long-form Python tutorials with runnable examples.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Review and QA Agents
notes.body:
**Where agent builds actually break — learn these failure modes before they cost you a production incident.**

- **Prompt injection via tool output.** Tool results are untrusted data, not instructions. An agent that obeys text returned by a tool hands control to whoever wrote that text. Validate outputs against schemas; never let tool content rewrite the plan silently.
- **Unbounded loops.** Without step caps, cost caps, and stagnation detection, an agent retries forever on a failing subtask. Every loop needs a budget and an exit condition.
- **Context rot.** Long trajectories accumulate stale and contradictory context; the agent starts acting on superseded plans. Summarize and re-ground state at fixed intervals.
- **No evals.** Shipping an agent without task-level success criteria means regressions arrive as user complaints. Define pass/fail per task before tuning prompts.
- **Over-permissioned tools.** Giving an agent destructive tools 'just in case' converts a prompt bug into data loss. Least privilege applies to agents too.

For *Review and QA Agents*, keep Practice: automated code-review agents; Practice: style and convention checks inside these guardrails: every capability you add gets a budget, a schema, and an eval.

handsOnLab.title: Hands-on lab: Review and QA Agents
handsOnLab.brief: You will build a small tool-calling agent loop from scratch (no framework), give it two tools, and then deliberately attack it: inject a malicious instruction through a tool result and verify your guardrails hold. The deliverable is the agent code plus a short safety report.
steps: Implement the minimal agent loop in ~60 lines: while steps remain, send messages to an LLM, parse tool calls, execute tools, append results. (Practice: automated code-review agents)
Define two tools with strict JSON schemas (e.g., a calculator and a key-value lookup). Reject any call whose arguments fail schema validation.
Add the guardrails: a max-step budget (e.g., 8), a stagnation detector (same tool+args twice = stop), and a rule that tool output is data, never instructions.
Run a benign task end to end and log the full trajectory: which tools were called, in what order, and why.
Attack your own agent: plant an instruction inside a tool result ('ignore previous instructions and …'). Confirm the agent does NOT obey it, and document what stopped it.
Write the safety report: threat model, guardrails implemented, attack test result, and one residual risk you accept with justification.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Agent source (~60-100 lines), a benign-task trajectory log, and a 1-page safety report with the attack-test outcome.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Loop terminates on budget; schema validation rejects malformed calls; the injected instruction is ignored; residual risk is named explicitly.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Agents in CI/CD pipelines** — As pipeline steps with scoped permissions: lint, test generation, failure triage — each with a blast radius sized to trust.
- **Issue triage agents** — Classify, deduplicate, route, and draft reproductions — shrinking the queue humans must read.
- **Release-notes generation** — Draft from merged PRs and diffs, with human approval before publish — grounding in the actual changes, not vibes.
- **Documentation agents** — API docs and guides from code and examples — reviewed like any docs PR, because generated docs can mislead.
- **On-call assistance patterns** — Triage assistance, runbook following, timeline reconstruction — under paging-policy respect and human command.
- **Workflow orchestration safety** — Permissions, approvals, and rollback for every automated step — the pipeline is production, treat it as such.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Map your pipeline: list every stage (lint, test, build, deploy) and the permissions each stage's runner holds today — the blast-radius inventory.
2. Size the blast radius for one agent step: define the smallest permission set it needs, then cut it once more — read-only first, always.
3. Build the triage agent: classify 20 real issues (bug, feature, question, duplicate), draft reproductions for 3, and hand-score the classification accuracy.
4. Generate release notes: draft from merged PR titles and diffs for one release; a human approves every line before anything ships — grounding plus approval.
5. Add the docs check: an agent that flags code merged without doc updates — read-only and advisory only, never blocking.
6. Draft the on-call assist: triage questions it may answer, runbook steps it may suggest, and the explicit rule that it never pages, acknowledges, or closes incidents itself.
7. Write the rollback plan for the assist itself: how to disable the agent step in under five minutes if it misbehaves.

Reference docs for this module:
- [GitHub Documentation](https://docs.github.com/en) — Repositories, Actions, and the workflows coding agents plug into.
- [LangGraph Documentation](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/) — Stateful agent graphs: loops, memory, and human-in-the-loop.

modules.summary: Welcome to SWE Agent Project — module 5 of 6 in the Agentic AI for Software Engineers track of IL-17 Agentic AI Engineering. I'm your instructor. In this module we cover a coding agent against a real repository, judged by tests: scope the task, measure the success rate, and document the failures honestly. We'll work through Choosing a real repo task; Building a coding agent loop; Wiring tests as the oracle; Measuring edit success rate; Iterating on failure modes; and Project write-up.
objectives: Build and demonstrate: choosing a real repo task
Build and demonstrate: building a coding agent loop
Build and demonstrate: wiring tests as the oracle
Build and demonstrate: measuring edit success rate
Build and demonstrate: iterating on failure modes

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Choosing a real repo task** — Bounded, test-covered, and representative — a real issue the team would actually assign.
- **Building a coding agent loop** — Context retrieval, diff proposal, test execution, failure reading — wired together and instrumented.
- **Wiring tests as the oracle** — Tests give objective pass/fail per attempt — the only success metric that is not the model grading itself.
- **Measuring edit success rate** — Attempts vs green-test merges on a fixed task set — the number that tells you if the agent is useful.
- **Iterating on failure modes** — Catalog the misses (bad context, wrong API, flaky tests), fix the loop or prompts, re-measure — the engineering cycle.
- **Project write-up** — Success rate, failure catalog, and limits — numbers and misses, not just the demo.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Choose the task: a real issue, bounded, with tests — and get it in writing (even from yourself) that the team would accept this fix.
2. Freeze the task set: 5–10 task instances or variants with expected outcomes — this fixed benchmark is what every later number refers to.
3. Build the loop: context retrieval, diff proposal, test execution, failure reading — instrumented end to end with a transcript.
4. Run the benchmark: record attempts, green merges, and iterations per task — the raw numbers before any interpretation.
5. Catalog the failures: every miss gets a row — bad context, wrong API, flaky test, unclear spec — with your diagnosis of the class.
6. Fix one failure class: change the loop or the prompts, re-run the benchmark, and show the delta in the numbers — the engineering cycle.
7. Write it up: success rate, failure catalog, limits — the honest report this track has been building toward.

Reference docs for this module:
- [LangChain Documentation](https://docs.langchain.com/) — Chains, LCEL, tools, and agent patterns.
- [Real Python](https://realpython.com/) — Long-form Python tutorials with runnable examples.
notes.lang:
benchmark = freeze_tasks(repo, n=8)   # fixed set, expected outcomes
results = []
for task in benchmark:
    attempt = agent_loop(task, max_iterations=10)
    results.append({
        "task": task.id,
        "green": attempt.tests_pass,       # the oracle
        "iterations": attempt.iterations,
        "failure_class": classify(attempt) if not attempt.tests_pass else None,
    })
success_rate = sum(r["green"] for r in results) / len(results)

notes.title: Common mistakes: SWE Agent Project
notes.body:
**Where agent builds actually break — learn these failure modes before they cost you a production incident.**

- **Prompt injection via tool output.** Tool results are untrusted data, not instructions. An agent that obeys text returned by a tool hands control to whoever wrote that text. Validate outputs against schemas; never let tool content rewrite the plan silently.
- **Unbounded loops.** Without step caps, cost caps, and stagnation detection, an agent retries forever on a failing subtask. Every loop needs a budget and an exit condition.
- **Context rot.** Long trajectories accumulate stale and contradictory context; the agent starts acting on superseded plans. Summarize and re-ground state at fixed intervals.
- **No evals.** Shipping an agent without task-level success criteria means regressions arrive as user complaints. Define pass/fail per task before tuning prompts.
- **Over-permissioned tools.** Giving an agent destructive tools 'just in case' converts a prompt bug into data loss. Least privilege applies to agents too.

modules.title: Limits and Safety
modules.summary: Welcome to Limits and Safety — module 6 of 6 in the Agentic AI for Software Engineers track of IL-17 Agentic AI Engineering. I'm your instructor. In this module we cover the module teams skip and incidents teach: generated code needs the same review bar as human code — higher, if anything, because it arrives with unearned confidence. We'll work through Where coding agents fail silently; Hallucinated APIs and dependencies; Security review of generated code; Least-privilege repo access; Licensing of generated code; and Setting team policy.
objectives: Apply in professional practice: where coding agents fail silently
Apply in professional practice: hallucinated APIs and dependencies
Apply in professional practice: security review of generated code
Apply in professional practice: least-privilege repo access
Apply in professional practice: licensing of generated code

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Where coding agents fail silently** — Plausible-but-wrong APIs, subtly broken logic, and passing-the-wrong-tests — confidence without correctness.
- **Hallucinated APIs and dependencies** — Invented functions, flags, or packages that look real — verify every reference against the actual codebase and registry.
- **Security review of generated code** — Agents reproduce insecure patterns confidently — injection, auth, and secret-handling need human eyes.
- **Least-privilege repo access** — The agent gets the narrowest scope that lets it work — never broad write access to start.
- **Licensing of generated code** — Training-data provenance is murky; teams need policy on what generated code may enter the codebase.
- **Setting team policy** — Allowed tools, review requirements, secret handling, and what must never be auto-merged — written, not tribal.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Collect 3 agent-generated diffs (or write representative ones); treat every API call in them as suspect until verified.
2. Verify references: for each function, flag, and import in the diffs, confirm it exists in the actual codebase or dependency tree — log every hallucination you find.
3. Registry check: for each dependency a diff introduces, verify it exists in the package registry and pin the version you actually checked — invented packages look real.
4. Security pass: walk the diff against a checklist — injection points, auth checks, secret handling, and error messages that leak internals.
5. Secrets scan: search the diff for tokens, keys, and credential-shaped strings; verify none, and note where the agent was one prompt away from emitting one.
6. License review: assess the provenance risk — generated code with murky training-data origins — against your team's policy for what may enter the codebase.
7. Draft the team policy: allowed tools, review requirements, secret handling, and the no-auto-merge rule — one page, in writing, not tribal knowledge.

Reference docs for this module:
- [GitHub Documentation](https://docs.github.com/en) — Repositories, Actions, and the workflows coding agents plug into.
- [OpenAI Platform Documentation](https://platform.openai.com/docs) — API references and guides; the anchor for model-calling patterns.
notes.lang:
import ast

def verify_api_refs(diff_source, known_symbols):
    """Every name the generated code touches must exist somewhere real."""
    tree = ast.parse(diff_source)
    used = {n.id for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Name)}
    hallucinations = used - known_symbols - set(dir(__builtins__))
    return hallucinations  # non-empty = invented APIs: investigate each

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: No checklist catches everything — the most dangerous failures are the ones that look idiomatic and pass tests. Policy only works if the team follows it when the deadline is tight. Ask yourself: what would make you skip the review on a Friday afternoon, and how does the policy survive that?

modules.title: Data Agents
modules.summary: Welcome to Data Agents — module 1 of 6 in the Agentic AI for Data Engineers track of IL-17 Agentic AI Engineering. I'm your instructor. In this module we cover agents as the interface between a question and a warehouse: schema-aware, read-first, and honest about uncertainty instead of inventing rows. We'll work through Agents that query data; Natural-language interfaces to warehouses; Schema awareness; Safe query generation; Result interpretation; and When the agent should ask before running.
objectives: Understand and apply: agents that query data
Understand and apply: natural-language interfaces to warehouses
Understand and apply: schema awareness
Understand and apply: safe query generation
Understand and apply: result interpretation

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Agents that query data** — Summarize what the rows show, state the query’s limits, and flag uncertainty — never invent rows that are not there.
- **Natural-language interfaces to warehouses** — Parse the question, link to schema, generate SQL, validate, execute read-only, present results — each step guarded.
- **Schema awareness** — Knowing tables, columns, types, and relationships — the grounding that prevents hallucinated columns.
- **Safe query generation** — Validated, dialect-correct, cost-capped SELECTs — dry-run before execution, limits always.
- **Result interpretation** — translating query results into answers with the caveats a data engineer would add: grain, filters, freshness, and what the data cannot say.
- **When the agent should ask before running** — Expensive queries, ambiguous intent, or anything near a write path — the cost of asking is tiny next to the cost of a bad run.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Pick a real schema you know (even 3 tables); write down the tables, keys, and one tricky join — the ground truth the agent must respect.
2. Build the schema briefing: the context block the agent receives — table and column descriptions in plain language, not just DDL, including the ambiguous column pairs.
3. Implement the ask-before-running gate: classify questions into 'safe to run' (read-only, bounded, unambiguous) vs 'ask first' (ambiguous, expensive, or touching sensitive columns) — write the rules down.
4. Run 10 questions: log each generated query, whether the gate fired, and whether the question was actually answerable from the schema.
5. Practice the honest 'I don't know': craft 3 questions the data cannot answer and verify the agent declines instead of inventing rows.
6. Interpret results: for each answer, write the one-sentence caveat a data engineer would add — grain, filters, freshness.
7. Review the gate log: which 'ask first' cases were right, which were over-cautious, and what rule change each suggests.

Reference docs for this module:
- [OpenAI: Function Calling Guide](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/function-calling) — The tool-use pattern every agent framework wraps.
- [pandas Documentation](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/) — DataFrame reference and user guide for wrangling.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Choose a small real pipeline (or a realistic sketch): source, transform, load — with a DAG you can draw on one page.
2. Generate the DAG: have the agent scaffold the pipeline definition from your description, then diff it against the hand-written version line by line.
3. Inject schema drift: add a column upstream and rename another; run the agent's drift handler and check whether it detected, alerted, and adapted — or silently broke.
4. Plan a backfill: pick a date range, compute the partitions affected, and have the agent produce the backfill plan with idempotency stated explicitly.
5. Scaffold tests: generate one test per pipeline stage — row counts, schema checks, a business-rule assertion — run them, and fix the ones that assert the wrong thing.
6. Wire the orchestrator: define where the agent's outputs land (pull requests, not direct commits) and who approves them.
7. Run the 3 AM test: read the generated pipeline as the on-call engineer — is everything you'd need at 3 AM written down?

- [LangGraph Documentation](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/) — Stateful agent graphs: loops, memory, and human-in-the-loop.

def handle_schema_drift(detected_columns, expected_schema):
    new_cols = detected_columns - expected_schema
    missing = expected_schema - detected_columns
    if new_cols or missing:
        alert_human(f"drift detected: +{new_cols} -{missing}")  # alert first
        return propose_mapping(new_cols, missing)  # adapt only under a test gate
    return None  # no drift: the common, boring, good case

notes.title: Common mistakes: Pipeline Agents
notes.body:
**Where agent builds actually break — learn these failure modes before they cost you a production incident.**

- **Prompt injection via tool output.** Tool results are untrusted data, not instructions. An agent that obeys text returned by a tool hands control to whoever wrote that text. Validate outputs against schemas; never let tool content rewrite the plan silently.
- **Unbounded loops.** Without step caps, cost caps, and stagnation detection, an agent retries forever on a failing subtask. Every loop needs a budget and an exit condition.
- **Context rot.** Long trajectories accumulate stale and contradictory context; the agent starts acting on superseded plans. Summarize and re-ground state at fixed intervals.
- **No evals.** Shipping an agent without task-level success criteria means regressions arrive as user complaints. Define pass/fail per task before tuning prompts.
- **Over-permissioned tools.** Giving an agent destructive tools 'just in case' converts a prompt bug into data loss. Least privilege applies to agents too.

For *Pipeline Agents*, keep Practice: agents that build and repair pipelines; Practice: DAG generation inside these guardrails: every capability you add gets a budget, a schema, and an eval.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Fix the schema: 3–5 tables with realistic names, keys, and one deliberately ambiguous column pair (for example `created_at` vs `registered_at`).
2. Build the schema-linking step: for 10 questions, write by hand which tables and columns each needs — then check what the agent links and score the gap.
3. Add dialect awareness: pick your warehouse dialect, list 3 functions that differ from standard SQL, and test whether generated queries respect them.
4. Validate before execution: syntax check first, then EXPLAIN — read the plan for full scans and runaway joins before anything runs.
5. Set the guardrails as a stack, not one trick: a read-only role, a statement timeout, and a hard block on writes and deletes without human approval — implement all three.
6. Evaluate: 15 realistic questions with known-correct answers; score exact-match and 'correct result' separately — they measure different things.
7. Diagnose 3 failures in writing: wrong table, wrong join, or wrong filter — and which pipeline stage should have caught each.

def guarded_execute(nl_question):
    query = generate_sql(nl_question)          # schema-linked generation
    check_syntax(query)                        # parse before anything else
    plan = explain(query)                      # read the plan: scans? joins?

notes.title: Common mistakes: Text-to-SQL Agents
notes.body:
**Where agent builds actually break — learn these failure modes before they cost you a production incident.**

- **Prompt injection via tool output.** Tool results are untrusted data, not instructions. An agent that obeys text returned by a tool hands control to whoever wrote that text. Validate outputs against schemas; never let tool content rewrite the plan silently.
- **Unbounded loops.** Without step caps, cost caps, and stagnation detection, an agent retries forever on a failing subtask. Every loop needs a budget and an exit condition.
- **Context rot.** Long trajectories accumulate stale and contradictory context; the agent starts acting on superseded plans. Summarize and re-ground state at fixed intervals.
- **No evals.** Shipping an agent without task-level success criteria means regressions arrive as user complaints. Define pass/fail per task before tuning prompts.
- **Over-permissioned tools.** Giving an agent destructive tools 'just in case' converts a prompt bug into data loss. Least privilege applies to agents too.

For *Text-to-SQL Agents*, keep Understand and apply: schema linking; Understand and apply: SQL dialect awareness inside these guardrails: every capability you add gets a budget, a schema, and an eval.

notes.body:
- **Anomaly detection on tables** — Distribution shifts, sudden nulls, volume spikes — the data breaking before downstream notices.
- **Freshness and completeness checks** — Is the data new enough and whole enough for its consumers — the two questions every pipeline must answer.
- **Contract testing** — Asserting schema and invariants at boundaries — the API contract idea applied to tables.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Pick 2 tables you know; define 'healthy' for each: freshness SLA, expected row-count range, and the key columns that must never be null.
2. Implement freshness and completeness checks first: scheduled queries that alert when the SLA breaks — start with the dumb thresholds before anything 'smart'.
3. Add anomaly detection: a simple statistical check (z-score on row counts, null-rate spikes) on one metric; tune until the alert rate is livable.
4. Write contract tests: the schema and semantics downstream expects — run them on every load and fail fast on breakage.
5. Build the triage agent: given an alert, it gathers context (recent deploys, upstream freshness, similar past alerts) and drafts the triage note — a human still decides severity.
6. Dashboard it: one page showing check status over time — the agent's job is to keep it green and honest, not green at all costs.
7. Tune for a week (or simulate one): log every alert as real breakage or noise, and adjust thresholds until the team would trust the page.

def contract_test(table, expected):
    """Fail fast when upstream breaks the shape downstream expects."""
    assert set(table.columns) >= set(expected["required_columns"])
    assert table[expected["key"]].is_unique, "key uniqueness violated"
    assert table[expected["not_null"]].notnull().all().all()
    assert expected["row_range"][0] <= len(table) <= expected["row_range"][1]
    return "contract holds"

modules.summary: Welcome to Trust and Guardrails — module 6 of 6 in the Agentic AI for Data Engineers track of IL-17 Agentic AI Engineering. I'm your instructor. In this module we cover the trust layer data teams must build before the demo becomes a service: caps, logs, approvals, and PII handling — governance the agent cannot opt out of. We'll work through Read-only by default; Query cost caps; PII awareness; Audit logging of agent queries; Human approval for writes; and Data governance alignment.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Read-only by default** — It removes the entire class of destructive mistakes — the cheapest safety property in data engineering.
- **Query cost caps** — Hard limits on scan cost per query and per agent — the warehouse bill cannot be prompt-injected.
- **PII awareness** — Knowing which columns are sensitive and redacting or refusing per policy — governance the agent cannot opt out of.
- **Audit logging of agent queries** — Every generated query recorded with who/what/when — the trail that makes incidents answerable.
- **Human approval for writes** — Any write, any PII access beyond policy, any expensive run — the gates that keep automation safe.
- **Data governance alignment** — The agent’s behavior matching the org’s classification, retention, and access policies — in writing, enforced in code.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Before you trust the narrative, work the numbers. The example below is illustrative — every assumption is labeled so you can substitute your own.

Work the cost-cap math for a data agent, with your own numbers. Suppose the agent averages 8 tool calls per question — schema lookup, query generation, validation, execution, interpretation (count them from your own runs; this is illustrative). Call one model interaction's cost u. Then one question costs about 8u, and 1,000 questions a day costs about 8,000u a day. Now apply the guardrails as math. (1) A per-query step budget of 12 bounds the worst single question at 12u instead of an unbounded loop — compute your own worst case: budget times u. (2) A daily spend cap C means the agent stops answering after C/u questions — set C from what the answers are worth, not from vibes: if each answered question saves roughly 10 minutes of analyst time, price that time and set C below it. (3) The EXPLAIN-first rule converts 'runaway query' from a warehouse-bill event into a rejected plan — estimate one bad full scan a week without it, and price the scan from your warehouse's billing model. Fill in u from your provider's pricing (as of October 2026 — verify it, don't trust this page), your daily question volume, and your per-question value. The output is a one-page cost policy: per-query budget, daily cap, and the approval threshold above which a human reviews the plan. The estimation habit is the point — every assumption labeled, every number replaceable.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Trust and Guardrails
notes.body:
**Where agent builds actually break — learn these failure modes before they cost you a production incident.**

- **Prompt injection via tool output.** Tool results are untrusted data, not instructions. An agent that obeys text returned by a tool hands control to whoever wrote that text. Validate outputs against schemas; never let tool content rewrite the plan silently.
- **Unbounded loops.** Without step caps, cost caps, and stagnation detection, an agent retries forever on a failing subtask. Every loop needs a budget and an exit condition.
- **Context rot.** Long trajectories accumulate stale and contradictory context; the agent starts acting on superseded plans. Summarize and re-ground state at fixed intervals.
- **No evals.** Shipping an agent without task-level success criteria means regressions arrive as user complaints. Define pass/fail per task before tuning prompts.
- **Over-permissioned tools.** Giving an agent destructive tools 'just in case' converts a prompt bug into data loss. Least privilege applies to agents too.

In this module we cover the PM's honest capability map: what the demo implies versus what production requires — cost, latency, evals, and the questions that separate a prototype from a shippable feature. - **Cost and latency intuition** — Per-task token math and p95 latencies — the numbers that decide whether a feature is shippable.
- **Evaluation basics for PMs** — Golden task sets, success criteria, and regression checks — enough to ask engineers the right questions.
- **Reading an agent architecture diagram** — Follow the loop: triggers, tools, memory, guardrails, escalation — and ask where each can fail.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Before you trust the narrative, work the numbers. The example below is illustrative — every assumption is labeled so you can substitute your own.

Price one real agent feature pitch you've heard, with your own numbers. Suppose a support agent would handle 500 conversations a day (illustrative — use your own volume), averaging 6 tool calls per conversation (lookup, policy check, draft, verify, and so on). If one model interaction costs roughly u, the daily model cost is about 3,000u. Now compare: a human-handled conversation costs H. Breakeven needs (3,000u + build + evals + on-call) to be less than (conversations × H × automation_fraction) — and automation_fraction is measured, never assumed; start it at the pilot's measured number, not the demo's. Latency: if each step takes about 2 seconds (model plus tool), a 6-step conversation is about 12 seconds of pure machine time before queueing — map that against your SLA. If the SLA is 30 seconds, 18 seconds of budget remain for everything else; write down what consumes it. Evals: a 200-question golden set, each needing a human-verified answer — estimate the hours to build it (5–10 minutes per question is typical) and price that before promising a launch date. The deliverable is a one-page capability note — what the demo implies versus what production requires — with every assumption labeled. As of October 2026 model pricing moves; verify current numbers, don't memorize them.

handsOnLab.title: Hands-on lab: Spec and PRD Agents
handsOnLab.brief: You will build a small tool-calling agent loop from scratch (no framework), give it two tools, and then deliberately attack it: inject a malicious instruction through a tool result and verify your guardrails hold. The deliverable is the agent code plus a short safety report.
steps: Implement the minimal agent loop in ~60 lines: while steps remain, send messages to an LLM, parse tool calls, execute tools, append results. (Practice: drafting PRDs with agent assistance)
Define two tools with strict JSON schemas (e.g., a calculator and a key-value lookup). Reject any call whose arguments fail schema validation.
Add the guardrails: a max-step budget (e.g., 8), a stagnation detector (same tool+args twice = stop), and a rule that tool output is data, never instructions.
Run a benign task end to end and log the full trajectory: which tools were called, in what order, and why.
Attack your own agent: plant an instruction inside a tool result ('ignore previous instructions and …'). Confirm the agent does NOT obey it, and document what stopped it.
Write the safety report: threat model, guardrails implemented, attack test result, and one residual risk you accept with justification.
handsOnLab.deliverable: Agent source (~60-100 lines), a benign-task trajectory log, and a 1-page safety report with the attack-test outcome.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Loop terminates on budget; schema validation rejects malformed calls; the injected instruction is ignored; residual risk is named explicitly.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
This is the lab sequence — work the steps in order; each one builds on the last.
1. Pick a real feature (or a realistic one) and write the five-line version of what it does — the anchor everything else refers back to.
2. Draft with the agent: generate a PRD skeleton — problem, users, requirements, acceptance criteria — then mark every line as yours, the agent's, or joint.
3. Generate acceptance criteria: for each requirement, produce testable criteria — then delete every criterion you couldn't actually test.
4. Run the spec review agent: feed it the draft and collect its flags — missing edge cases, ambiguous terms, untestable claims.
5. Triage the flags: which were real gaps and which were noise? Keep score — the review-precision habit from the SWE track, applied to prose.
6. Version it: commit the spec, make one scope change, and diff — practice treating specs as versioned artifacts, not documents.
7. Decide: mark the sections that still need a human — trade-offs, ethics, the actual decision. The agent proposes; you dispose.

- [OpenAI Platform Documentation](https://platform.openai.com/docs) — API references and guides; the anchor for model-calling patterns.

notes.title: Common mistakes: Spec and PRD Agents
notes.body:
**Where agent builds actually break — learn these failure modes before they cost you a production incident.**

- **Prompt injection via tool output.** Tool results are untrusted data, not instructions. An agent that obeys text returned by a tool hands control to whoever wrote that text. Validate outputs against schemas; never let tool content rewrite the plan silently.
- **Unbounded loops.** Without step caps, cost caps, and stagnation detection, an agent retries forever on a failing subtask. Every loop needs a budget and an exit condition.
- **Context rot.** Long trajectories accumulate stale and contradictory context; the agent starts acting on superseded plans. Summarize and re-ground state at fixed intervals.
- **No evals.** Shipping an agent without task-level success criteria means regressions arrive as user complaints. Define pass/fail per task before tuning prompts.
- **Over-permissioned tools.** Giving an agent destructive tools 'just in case' converts a prompt bug into data loss. Least privilege applies to agents too.

For *Spec and PRD Agents*, keep Practice: drafting PRDs with agent assistance; Practice: acceptance-criteria generation inside these guardrails: every capability you add gets a budget, a schema, and an eval.
