scenarios.title: Designing a support agent
scenarios.context: You must design a customer-support agent that can look up orders, issue refunds up to $50, and escalate the rest. Whiteboard time.

steps.prompt: How do you scope the agent’s tools?

options.text: One broad tool with full database access
options.why: A god-tool violates least privilege — a model mistake becomes a database incident.

options.text: Narrow typed tools: order lookup (read), refund (capped at $50, logged), escalate-to-human
options.why: Least-privilege tool design bounds the blast radius; the refund cap and escalation path encode the policy in the tool contracts.

options.text: No tools — the model answers from training
options.why: Without tools the agent cannot see orders or act — it would hallucinate order statuses.

steps.prompt: The agent sometimes loops re-checking the same order. Fix?

options.text: Give it more steps
options.why: More budget feeds the loop — the failure is missing termination logic, not missing steps.

options.text: Add stopping conditions: step budget, no-repeat-observation rule, and escalate on stall
options.why: Stopping conditions come first in the module for exactly this reason — detect the stall and hand to a human.

options.text: Use a bigger model
options.why: A bigger model can loop just as expensively — control flow, not capability, is the fix.

steps.prompt: How do you evaluate before launch?

options.text: A few manual tries
options.why: Manual vibes do not catch trajectory regressions — you need a harness.

options.text: A small eval harness: task success, tool-call efficiency, refund-policy adherence, escalation correctness
options.why: The evaluation module’s recipe: success plus path quality, efficiency, and safety-constraint adherence on a fixed task set.

options.text: Vendor benchmark scores
options.why: Benchmarks measure base models, not your refund-capped support agent on your policies.

scenarios.title: The warehouse agent request
scenarios.context: A data team wants an agent that answers business questions against the warehouse. The warehouse holds PII and production tables.

options.text: Read-only access with query validation and audit logging
options.why: Read-only by default is the module’s non-negotiable: validate SQL, dry-run with EXPLAIN, cap cost, log everything.

options.text: Full access for speed of iteration
options.why: A model with write access to production tables is an incident waiting for a prompt.

options.text: No guardrails until the pilot ends
options.why: Guardrails are cheapest before the demo becomes a service — retrofitting trust is harder.

steps.prompt: The agent invents rows when data is missing. What’s the design fix?

options.text: Tell it to try harder
options.why: Prompt pleading does not fix a missing honesty mechanism.

options.text: Schema-aware grounding: require queries to return real rows, teach ‘I don’t know’ as a valid terminal state, verify against results
options.why: The data-agents module demands honesty about uncertainty — the agent must say when the data is not there instead of inventing rows.

options.text: Hide the missing-data cases
options.why: Hiding gaps corrupts downstream decisions — the worst outcome.

steps.prompt: Someone asks the agent for customer PII. Response?

options.text: Comply — the user asked
options.why: PII awareness is a governance requirement; the agent cannot opt out of it.

options.text: Refuse or redact per the data-classification policy, and log the attempt
options.why: Governance alignment: classification policy decides, audit trail records — the trust layer working as designed.

options.text: Answer but warn the user
options.why: A warning does not satisfy PII handling obligations — policy, not courtesy, governs.

scenarios.title: The team rollout decision
scenarios.context: Your pilot: an agent that drafts release notes from merged PRs. Four weeks in, engineers like it but you spot fabricated changelog entries twice.

steps.prompt: How do you measure the pilot honestly?

options.text: Survey vibes only
options.why: Liking is not measurement — you need time saved with a baseline, quality deltas, and cost per task.

options.text: Time saved vs the manual baseline, error/fabrication rate, adoption, and cost per assisted task — plus counter-metrics
options.why: The metrics module’s recipe: honest baselines, quality deltas, and the counter-metrics that catch what headlines hide.

options.text: Lines of notes generated
options.why: Volume without quality is a vanity metric — fabricated entries make it actively harmful.

options.text: Expand — engineers like it
options.why: Fabricated changelog entries are a trust defect; expanding spreads the defect.

options.text: Pause expansion: fix grounding (require PR-diff citations), add a human approval gate, re-pilot — then decide on numbers
options.why: The rollout playbook’s expand-or-stop decision is made on guardrailed metrics — fix the failure mode, re-measure, then decide.

options.text: Stop forever — agents don’t work
options.why: One fixable failure mode is not a verdict on the approach — it is what pilots are for.

blocks.body: **Perceive → reason → act**: observe state, decide, call a tool. **ReAct**: interleave thought and action explicitly. **Plan-and-execute**: decompose first, then run the plan. **Stopping first**: step budgets, no-repeat rules, stall escalation.
**Short-term**: conversation history, budgeted. **Summarization**: compress old turns. **Vector recall**: semantic lookup of past steps. **State stores/checkpoints**: resume long runs safely.

Default to **one** agent. Earn two with: **supervisor/worker** (decompose + delegate), **role specialization** with handoffs, **debate/critique** for quality. Watch: coordination failure modes and communication overhead.
Score **success + trajectory**: task completion, tool-call efficiency, failure recovery, safety adherence. Build the **small eval harness** before the demo becomes a service.

- JSON schemas: typed, machine-readable
- Validate args before executing — never trust model output
- Tool-choice controls: auto / required / none
- Structured errors the model can reason about

- Narrow tools: one job each
- Read-only by default for data agents
- Human approval for writes, refunds, deletes
- Budget tool calls per run; audit-log everything

- Schema linking: ground terms in real tables/columns
- Dialect awareness for the target warehouse
- Reject non-SELECT (no writes/deletes) by default
- EXPLAIN-plan sanity check; row LIMIT auto-applied

- Query cost caps
- PII awareness and redaction
- Audit logging of every agent query
- Human approval for any write path
- Evaluate on realistic schemas, not toy ones

- One workflow, tightly scoped
- Guardrails and approvals designed first
- Metrics: time saved vs baseline, quality deltas, cost per task
- Counter-metrics for what the headline hides

- **Expand or stop** on the numbers, not the demo
- Governance: access controls, classification, audit trails, written policy
- Rollback plan before launch
- Report impact to leadership with honest baselines
Perceive (tools/state) → reason (plan) → act (tool call) → observe → repeat. Every agent is this loop with different furniture.
Name, description, JSON schema, side effects declared, idempotency noted. Vague tools produce vague agents.
Short-term: the context window (compact/summarize). Long-term: vector store, files, databases. Memory is retrieval with a write policy.
Max steps, goal predicates, confidence thresholds, human approval gates. An agent without a stop condition is a liability.
Tools get minimum scope: read-only where possible, sandboxed execution, approval for irreversible actions.

cheatSheets.title: Multi-agent — only when one is provably insufficient

blocks.body: Can one agent with good tools and context do it? If yes, multi-agent adds coordination failure modes for no gain.
Supervisor/workers (decompose), pipeline (sequential specialists), debate (adversarial review), market (bidding). Match pattern to task structure.
Message bloat, blame diffusion, cascading errors, coordination overhead. Log every inter-agent message.
Shared blackboard state, explicit handoff protocols, single owner per subtask. Ambiguity compounds across agents.

cheatSheets.title: Agent evaluation — trajectory, not just success

blocks.body: Did it achieve the goal? Necessary but insufficient — a lucky agent and a good agent both succeed once.
Steps taken vs. optimal, tool efficiency, error recovery. Log and score the path, not just the destination.
Did it respect scope, ask before irreversible actions, avoid prompt-injection traps? Red-team the agent, not just the model.
Tokens per task, wall-clock time, tool-call counts. An agent 10× pricier than the manual process needs 10× the value.
Copilot Studio / Foundry with scoped connectors: prove value fast, with guardrails built in.
When low-code limits hit (custom tools, eval rigor, cost control), move to LangGraph/pro-code with the same eval suite.
Trace every run: prompts, tool calls, latencies, costs. AgentOps = debugging production agents.
Draw the loop, the tools, the memory, the stops, the evals — and defend each tradeoff. If you can't draw it, you can't ship it.

answerBank.q: Design an agent system on a whiteboard: a research assistant over internal docs.
answerBank.a: Scope: read-only Q&A with citations over a fixed corpus. Loop: perceive the question, plan retrieval (hybrid search + rerank), generate with citation grounding, stop on answered-or-escalate with a step budget. Tools: search_docs (typed schema), no writes. Memory: conversation summary plus vector recall of past findings. Evals: golden Q&A set measuring citation faithfulness and task success, plus adversarial ‘unanswerable’ cases. Tradeoffs: hybrid retrieval costs latency but buys precision; citations add tokens but make answers auditable; human escalation bounds the hallucination risk.

answerBank.q: When would you NOT use an agent?
answerBank.a: When the task is deterministic and single-step — a direct function call is cheaper, faster, and debuggable. When latency budgets forbid multi-step loops. When the action space cannot be made safe (no guardrails possible). And when evaluation is impossible: if I cannot measure success, I cannot ship an agent responsibly. One agent is the default; zero agents is the default for deterministic work.

answerBank.q: How do you evaluate an agent beyond ‘did it succeed’?
answerBank.a: Trajectory quality: steps taken vs a reasonable minimum, tool-call efficiency, and whether it recovered from failures gracefully. Safety adherence: did it respect least-privilege, stay read-only, escalate when stalled. Cost: tokens and latency per task. I’d build a small harness over a fixed task set with these dimensions scored, because an agent that succeeds in 40 wasteful risky steps is worse than one succeeding in 5 safe ones.

answerBank.q: A coding agent keeps introducing subtle bugs. How do you make it trustworthy?
answerBank.a: Tests as the oracle: the loop is generate, run the test suite, read the failure, repeat — no merge without green tests. Scope edits with diffs as the unit of work; keep repo context via retrieval rather than dumping the codebase. Add a human review gate that never moves, least-privilege repo access, and measure edit success rate over time. Generated code gets the same review bar as human code — higher, because it arrives with unearned confidence.

answerBank.q: How do you keep a text-to-SQL agent from damaging the warehouse?
answerBank.a: Read-only by default: reject anything that is not SELECT/WITH, validate against the schema, run EXPLAIN as a sanity check, auto-apply row LIMITs, and cap query cost. Schema linking grounds terms in real tables so it cannot hallucinate columns. Every query is audit-logged; any write path needs explicit human approval. PII columns are classified and redacted per policy.

answerBank.q: Your agent pilot shows good vibes but unclear value. What do you measure?
answerBank.a: Time saved measured against the manual baseline — not self-reported, observed. Quality deltas: error rates before and after. Adoption: who actually uses it weekly. Cost per assisted task: tokens plus infra. And counter-metrics: what got worse (review burden, escalation volume). The expand-or-stop decision is made on these numbers, with the failure catalog attached — vibes inform, metrics decide.

answerBank.q: Low-code vs pro-code for an agent: how do you choose?
answerBank.a: Low-code when the workflow fits the platform’s connectors, the customization ceiling is comfortably above the need, and speed matters more than control. Graduate to pro-code when you hit the ceiling, when scale costs balloon, when governance needs exceed the platform, or when lock-in risk becomes strategic. The skill is knowing the ceiling before you build — assess fit honestly up front, and design the escape path (exportable logic, owned data) from day one.

glossary.definition: Perceive → reason → act → observe: the primitive cycle of every AI agent.
The precise interface an agent sees: name, description, JSON schema, declared side effects.
Reasoning + Acting interleaved: the dominant agent prompting pattern.
Model emitting structured tool invocations validated against schemas.
Model Context Protocol: standard for exposing tools/data sources to models and agents.
Managing the agent's working set: compaction, clearing, retrieval, memory writes.
Summarizing long context to fit the window without losing task-critical state.
The full sequence of an agent's thoughts, tool calls, and observations — the unit of evaluation.
Multi-agent design: a coordinator decomposes tasks and delegates to worker agents.
Shared state all agents read/write — the coordination mechanism preventing message chaos.
Tools scoped to minimum necessary power; read-only defaults; approval for irreversible actions.
Malicious instructions smuggled via tool outputs/data that the agent treats as commands.
Tracing, observability, and debugging discipline for production agent systems.
The planned move from low-code agents to pro-code when scale/customization demands it.
Coding agent operating on repositories: plan, edit, test, iterate — with guardrails.

faq.q: When should I NOT build an agent?
faq.a: When a script, a pipeline, or a single LLM call solves it. Agents earn their complexity only for multi-step tasks with branching decisions and tool interaction. The course's first test is 'prove one agent is insufficient' — before that, 'prove an agent is needed at all.'

faq.q: What's the hardest part of agent eval?
faq.a: Defining done: trajectory quality (efficiency, recovery, safety) matters as much as task success. Build the eval harness before the agent — it's the spec.

faq.q: How do I stop prompt injection?
faq.a: You don't, with one trick — defense in depth: instruction hierarchy, treating tool output as data, output validation, least-privilege tools, and human approval for irreversible actions.

faq.q: Low-code or pro-code for my first agent?
faq.a: Low-code (Copilot Studio/Foundry) to prove value with scoped connectors; graduate to pro-code (LangGraph) when you need custom tools, rigorous evals, or cost control. Plan the graduation path upfront.

faq.q: Why do agents need stopping conditions?
faq.a: Without step budgets and progress detection, agents loop forever on hard tasks — burning tokens and occasionally doing damage. Stops are safety features, not limitations.

faq.q: How is this different from IL-12's agent modules?
faq.a: IL-12 covers agents as one AI-engineering topic among many. IL-17 is the deep track: agent architectures, multi-agent systems, trajectory evals, AgentOps, and the whiteboard defense.

faq.q: What should I trace in production?
faq.a: Every run: prompts, tool calls with args/results, latencies, token costs, and the final trajectory. You can't debug what you can't replay.

tips: Follow the guided path in order — each module unlocks the next. The sequence is the curriculum; skipping ahead breaks the chain.

This course maps to AWS Certified AI Practitioner (AIF-C01) and Microsoft Certified: Azure AI Apps and Agents Developer Associate (AI-103) (independent preparation — no affiliation). Weight your drill time toward the heaviest exam domains shown in the cert gates.

The math modules (Prereq Math: Logic & Proof for Agentic AI Engineering, Prereq Math: Statistics & Probability for Agentic AI Engineering, Prereq Math: Discrete Mathematics for Agentic AI Engineering) are load-bearing — finish them before the applied modules that assume them.
Quiz-gated modules need 70%+ to unlock the next. When you miss a question, ask Noah to walk you through the miss Socratically before re-attempting.
Do each hands-on lab twice — once following the guide, once from a blank screen. The second pass is where the skill sticks.
This is a 325-hour course: at 10 focused hours a week it takes about 8 months. Short daily sessions beat weekend cramming — pace it like a semester.
